lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Welcome to our lesson, Unit 1: Being Alive. In this lesson we learn how to tell if something is alive or not alive. We do it because scientists look carefully and then say why. By the end, you will be able to point at a thing and say "that is living" or "that is not living" — and give a good reason. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are 4 steps. Step 1. Look around the room you are in. Tell me one thing you can see that you think is ALIVE, and one thing you think is NOT alive. A good answer names two things, like "my cat is alive, my chair is not alive." Take your time — there's no rush.

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this page is our Science Words page. These are the eight special words we use in Unit 1, Being Alive. Scientists always use exact words, so we will learn them too. By the end, you will be able to say each word, say what it means, and use it in your own sentence. All you need is your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. There are 4 steps. Here is step 1. Step 1: our first word is Living. Living means something that is alive. It grows, it eats, it drinks, and it breathes. A goat is living. You are living too! What I expect from you: say one living thing you can see near you right now, and tell me why it is living. 🌱

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Welcome to Unit 1, Being Alive! I am your teacher today. 🌱

This page is our unit overview. That means we look at the whole unit before we start, like looking at a map before a trip. We do it so you know what you will learn and nothing feels like a surprise. By the end of this activity you will be able to say what "living" means, and point at things around you and tell me if they are living or not living. What I expect from you: look around your room, think before you answer, and tell me your idea in your own words. Even a short answer is good, as long as it is your thinking. There is no need to write anything down unless you want to. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Step 1: The unit is called "Being Alive". Tell me what you already know about this. What does it mean when we say something is alive?

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today, and this page is called Visual Models. A visual model is a picture that helps an idea stick in your head. There are four pictures on your page, and each one shows a big idea from our unit "Being Alive". By the end, you will be able to look at anything around you and say if it is living or not living, and why. You need your eyes, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are four steps, one for each picture. Step one. Look at the first model on your screen. It is called "Living or Not Living?"

Look at the picture carefully. Then tell me one thing you SEE in it. Take your time — there's no rush.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text:
Hello! I am your teacher today. 👋

Here is what we are doing. This is Explore the Concept for Unit 1, Being Alive. You will learn how to tell if something is living or not living, and what living things need to stay alive. By the end, you will be able to look at anything around you and say "that is living" or "that is not living" — and say why. What you need: your eyes, a few things near you to look at, and your voice. A pencil and paper if you like drawing. A grown-up can sit with you. What I expect from you: answer with your own words, even if you are not sure. Say WHY, not just yes or no. Mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step one. Pick up something hard near you, like a stone, a spoon, or a cup. Look at it. Now ask it my four questions in your head: Does it grow? Does it eat? Does it drink? Can it have babies? Tell me what you picked, and your answer: is it living or not living?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Welcome to Learn the Method! 🌱

A method is just the way scientists do a job, step by step. Today's method is called Watch a Seed Grow. We do it because it shows us something important: a seed is a living thing, because it grows. Here is what I expect from you. First you guess what will happen. Then you look very carefully. Then you tell me if your guess was right. Good scientists always do those three things. You will need a pencil and paper, a seed (a bean is perfect), a cup, some cotton wool or soil, and water. Ask your grown-up to help you get them. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Make a prediction. A prediction is your best guess before you start. Tell me what you think will happen to the bean seed after you plant it and water it for a few days. Take your time — there's no rush. What do you predict?

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing Worked Examples. A worked example is a question with the thinking shown. We look at one question, you have a go, and then I show you how a scientist would say the answer out loud. This helps you learn the words to use, not just the answer. What I expect from you: try each one first, even if you are not sure. Then say your answer in a full sentence, like "A goat is living because..." That "because" part is the science! We will do four examples together. Here comes question one. A goat eats grass. It drinks water. It grows bigger. Is a goat living, or not living? Tell me your answer, and say why.

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Welcome to Guided Practice! This is where you use what you learned about living and not living things. We do it because practising helps the ideas stick in your head. By the end, you will be able to look at anything and say "living" or "not living" — and say why. You need your voice, and a pencil if you like to write your answers down. A grown-up can sit with you if you want. There are twelve questions on this page. We will do them one at a time, starting easy. What I expect from you: don't just say living or not living — always tell me WHY. Two words like "it grows" is a great answer. Here comes question one. A goat eats grass, drinks water and grows bigger. Is a goat living or not living? Tell me why.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Welcome! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Science Words page. On this page we learn the special words for Unit 1: Being Alive. We learn them so you can say WHY something is alive, not just guess. By the end, you will be able to use three science words all by yourself. You need your ears, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one! Step one: say this word out loud with me — Living. Living means something that is alive. It grows, eats, drinks and breathes. Now tell me one living thing you can see near you right now.

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text: Great question! Let's start. Today we are doing the Living or Not Living Hunt. That means you go looking around your home, like a scientist, and find real things to sort into two groups: living and not living. We do this because scientists learn by looking closely at real things, not just by reading. By the end you will be able to point at a thing and say why it is living or not living. You will need a pencil, some paper, and your eyes. You can ask your grown-up to help you. There are 5 steps. I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Take your paper and draw a line down the middle. On the left side write "Living". On the right side write "Not Living". Tell me when your paper is ready. 🙂

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Welcome to Science Fluency! This is our quick practice page. I ask you a short question, you answer fast, and we see how well the Unit 1 ideas are stuck in your head. Why we do it: quick answers show that you really know something, not just remember it for a minute. What I expect from you: try to answer in one short sentence, and say WHY. For example, "It is living because it grows." Take your time — there's no rush. There are 3 rounds, with a few questions in each. Ready? Here comes question one. A goat eats grass. It drinks water. It grows bigger. Is a goat living or not living?

games.label: Games
games.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Games page. A game here is a quick practice. I say a question, you pick the answer, and we see if it is right. We do this so the Unit 1 words stick in your head — living, non-living, animal, plant. By the end you will be able to look at a thing and say if it is alive, and say why. You need only your thinking brain and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. We will play 4 rounds. Here comes question one. Which one is alive? a camel, a rock, a metal spoon, or a plastic cup?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Welcome! This page is called Solve Real Problems. Here you use what you know about living things in real life — at home, at the market, out in nature. Why? Because science is not just words. It helps you understand the goat, the plant and your own body. You will need your voice, and a pencil if you like to write. There are six problems. I will give you one at a time. I expect you to answer in a sentence AND say why. The word "because" is your best friend today. Here comes question one. A hen has chicks. What does that tell you about the hen?

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explain Your Thinking."

In this activity you do not just say an answer. You say WHY. You will use our science words, like living, non-living, animal and plant. By the end, you will be able to explain how we know if something is alive. You need your thinking brain and your voice. A pencil is nice too, if you want to write. There are 4 questions. I will give you one at a time. I expect a full sentence, not just "yes" or "no" — tell me your answer AND your reason. Here comes question one. A mango tree does not walk about. Some children say that means it is not alive. Are they right? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me why. Take your time — there's no rush.

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for The Lesson in Unit 2: Growing Plants. In this lesson we learn about plants. We will find the parts of a plant, learn what a plant needs, and see how a tiny seed becomes a big plant. By the end, you will be able to name the parts of a plant and say what each one does. 🌱

You need your eyes, your voice, and if you can, a real plant or a picture of one. A pencil is nice too. There are three steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look at a plant. It can be a real plant near you, a plant in the picture on your page, or one you remember. Tell me one thing you see. Take your time — there's no rush.

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Welcome to Unit 2: Growing Plants! 🌱

This page is our Unit Overview. That means we take a little look at everything we will learn before we start. We do it so you know where we are going, like looking at a map before a walk. By the end, you will be able to name the parts of a plant, say what a plant needs, and tell how a tiny seed becomes a big plant. You need just your eyes, your voice, and your thinking. There are 4 steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Tell me what you already know about plants. Say one thing — anything at all. A good answer is one short sentence, like "Plants are green" or "Plants grow in the garden."

Your turn!

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Welcome to Science Words for Unit 2, Growing Plants! On this page we learn the special words scientists use for plants. Knowing these words helps you talk about a plant like a real scientist. By the end you will be able to name the plant parts and say what each one does. You will need your eyes, your voice, and a pencil if you like drawing. Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, and then make your own little sentence with it. Short sentences are perfect. We have 3 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1 is three words about the parts of a plant. Here is the first one. Roots. The roots grow down under the soil. They drink water for the plant and hold it tight, like an anchor. Now say "roots" out loud, then make your own sentence with it. 🌱

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Welcome! Today we are exploring the parts of a plant. We will look at a real plant and find its four main parts. We do this because every part has its own job, just like your eyes and legs have jobs. By the end, you will be able to point at a plant and name each part out loud. You need a plant to look at — a plant in a pot, a flower, or even a tuft of grass from outside. A pencil and paper too, if you like drawing. Ask your grown-up to help you find one. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Find your plant and look at it slowly for a few moments. I expect you to tell me one thing you notice about it. Maybe its colour, its size, or its shape. Take your time — there's no rush.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Welcome to Visual Models! On this page you get pictures that help you see how a plant works. We are doing this because pictures make science easy to remember. By the end, you will be able to point at each plant part and say its name and its job. You need your eyes, the picture on your screen, and maybe a pencil and paper. There are three models on this page, so we will do three steps together. Step 1: Look at the first model, "The Parts of a Plant". Look at it slowly from the bottom to the top. Then tell me the names of the parts you can see. A good answer names four parts. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Welcome to Worked Examples! This page shows you eight little plant questions with their answers all worked out, like a teacher showing you how it is done. We do this so you learn how to think about a question, not just remember the answer. By the end, you will be able to name the plant parts and say what each one does. You need your eyes, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. That's all! There are 8 examples, and we will do one at a time. Here comes step one. Look at this question: Which part of a plant hides under the soil and drinks water? Say your answer out loud, then type it to me. I expect one plant word — and if you can add what it does, even better! 🌱

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Welcome to Guided Practice! Today we practise our plant questions together. This is where you show what you know about plants — their parts, and what they need to grow. We do it so the words stick in your head, like roots holding a plant tight. You will need your voice, and maybe a pencil to write. I expect you to try every question yourself, even if you are not sure. A good answer names the plant part AND says its job. Guessing is allowed — mistakes are how we learn. There are 12 questions. We go one at a time. Here comes question one. Which part of a plant hides under the soil and drinks water?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are learning the method called The Parts of a Plant. A method is just a way of doing something, step by step. We do this one so you can look at any plant and name its parts: roots, stem, leaves and flower. By the end you will be able to point at a real plant and say what each part does. You need your eyes, your voice, and a plant to look at. A plant in a pot, a tree outside, or even a tuft of grass is perfect. A grown-up can help you find one. There are three steps. Here comes step one. Step one: put the idea in your own words. Tell me the four parts of a plant, and one job for one of them. A good answer sounds like this: "The parts are... and the ... does ..."

Take your time — there's no rush.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is our Science Words page for Unit 2, Growing Plants. It is like a little helper card that holds all our important plant words in one place. We use it so the words stay in your head, and so you can say them out loud all by yourself. By the end you will be able to name the parts of a plant and say what each part does. You will need a pencil and paper. A plant near your home is lovely too, but not needed. Here is what I expect from you: try each step out loud, even if you are not sure. There are four steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Look at the word list on your page. Find these four words: roots, stem, leaves, flower. Say them out loud, starting from the bottom of the plant and going up. A good answer sounds like this: "roots, stem, leaves, flower." Tell me when you have said them.

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text: Today we are scientists, and our experiment is called Grow a Bean Seed. We are going to plant a bean and watch it wake up. A dry bean looks hard and still, but a tiny baby plant is asleep inside it. By the end you will be able to say what a seed needs, and you will see the roots and the shoot appear with your own eyes. Here is what I expect from you: guess first, look carefully every day, and draw or tell me what changed. A good scientist says what they SEE, not just what they hope. You will need a dry bean, a clear cup or jar, some cotton wool or soil, and a little water. Ask your grown-up to help you find them. There are six steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Go and collect your things — one dry bean, a clear cup, cotton wool or soil, and water. Tell me when you have them all. If you cannot find a bean, tell me and we will think of something else you can use.

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to your Games page! These are short, fun plant games. Each game gives you four quick questions about plants — their parts and what they need. We play these to make your plant words stick, so you can name roots, stem, leaves and flower without stopping to think. Here is what I expect from you: read the question, pick ONE answer, and tell me why you picked it. Even a small "why" is enough. Guessing is fine — we will talk it through together. We will play the first game, "Quick Match: Roots". It has 4 rounds. Ready? Here comes question one. Round 1: Which part holds the plant in the soil? Is it roots, flower, leaf, or petal?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome to Solve Real Problems! 🌱

On this page you use what you know about plants to solve real-life questions. They are like little puzzles from home, the market and outside. We do this because a scientist does not just remember words — a scientist uses them to work things out. By the end you will be able to name plant parts and explain what plants need, in your own words. You need your thinking brain, and a pencil if you like to write. A grown-up can help you read. There are 6 problems. Here comes question one. Problem 1: Name the four main parts of a plant. I expect four words from you. Start at the bottom, under the soil, and go up to the top. Take your time — there's no rush.

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Science Fluency. Fluency means saying the answer quickly, without stopping to think for a long time. We do it so the plant words stay strong in your head, like knowing your own name. By the end you will be able to name the plant parts fast and say what each one does. You do not need anything except your voice and your thinking brain. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 3 rounds, and 4 questions in each round. That is 12 questions in all. I will give you one question at a time, and I will wait for you. What I expect from you: try your own answer first, even if you are not sure. A good answer names the part AND says its job, like "the leaves, they catch the sunlight."

Here comes question one. Which part of a plant hides under the soil and drinks water?

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text: Welcome to Explain Your Thinking! In this activity you don't just say an answer — you say WHY you think it. That is what real scientists do. By the end you will be able to explain plant ideas in your own words, using words like roots, stem and leaves. All you need is your thinking, and a pencil if you want to write. There are 3 thinking questions. I will give you one at a time. What I expect from you: a short answer, and then the word "because" with your reason. Even one sentence is great. Here comes question one. A plant is kept in a dark cupboard. Someone waters it every day. Will it grow well? Tell me yes or no, and then say because...

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Welcome to Unit 3! This unit is called Ourselves. It is all about your own body — the parts, the five senses, and how to keep clean and healthy. Today we start on the Unit Overview page. That means we look at what we will learn, and we try a little warm-up with our own body. By the end you will be able to touch and name five body parts out loud. You need just two things: your body, and your voice. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. Here is what I expect from you: say each word out loud, not just in your head. And tell me when you have done each step. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Stand up. Touch the top of your head and say the word "head" out loud. Tell me when you have done it. 🙂

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Welcome to our lesson! Today's lesson is called Ourselves. It is all about your own body — the parts you have, and the amazing senses that help you know the world. Why do we do it? Because your body is with you all day, and a good scientist starts by looking closely at what is right here. By the end, you will be able to name parts of your body and face, name the five senses, and say how to keep your body clean and healthy. You need just two things: your body, and your voice. A grown-up nearby can help you too. There are four parts to our lesson. Here comes part one. Part 1: Stand up, please. Touch the top of your head and say "head" out loud. Then touch your arms, your hands, your legs, and your feet — saying each name as you touch it. I expect you to say all five names out loud, not just in your head. Then type them back to me in the order you touched them. Take your time — there's no rush.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Welcome! Today we are scientists exploring our own bodies. On this page we explore the big ideas of Unit 3: our body parts, and our five senses. Here is how a scientist works. First we make a prediction, which means a good guess about what will happen. Then we test it. Then we see if we were right. What I expect from you: try each step with your own body, and tell me what you notice in your own words. There is no wrong answer when we are noticing! You need your body, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. That's all. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Stand up. Touch the top of your head and say "head". Then touch your arms, your hands, your legs, and your feet. Say each name out loud as you touch it. Tell me when you have done it, and tell me one part that was easy to find.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today we are using the Visual Models. A visual model is a picture that helps your brain hold an idea. There are four models in this unit, one for each big idea about our bodies. We are doing this so you can point, name and remember the parts of your body and your five senses. By the end, you will be able to name body parts and say which part does which job. You need your own body, a little space to stand up, and your voice. Ready? Here comes step one of four. Step 1: Look at the first model, The Parts of Our Body. Stand up. Touch each part and say its name out loud: head, arms, hands, legs, feet. I expect you to say all five names out loud while you touch them. Then tell me which one was the easiest to find. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Welcome! Today we are on Worked Examples for Unit 3, Ourselves. A worked example is a question with the thinking shown, like watching me solve it first. We do this so you learn HOW to think about your body and your senses, not just the answer. By the end you will be able to say which body part does each job. All you need is your own body and your voice. Ready? Let's start with something small. There are 8 examples. I will show you the first one, then you will try the next ones with me. Step 1 — watch me think. The question is: Which part of your body do you use to see? My thinking: I close my eyes. Now the room goes dark. So the part that sees must be my eyes. My answer: The eyes. We see with our eyes. Try closing your eyes for a moment, then open them. Tell me what you noticed. 👀

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are learning a method. A method is the way scientists do things, step by step. Our activity is called The Mystery Sound. You will close your eyes and use only your ears to find out what a sound is. We do this so you learn the science method: first you guess, then you look and listen carefully, then you check your guess. You need three things: your ears, a grown-up nearby to make the sound, and something to write or draw on. Here is what I expect from you. You must say your guess out loud BEFORE you listen. And you must tell me what you really heard, even if your guess was wrong. A wrong guess is fine. Mistakes are how we learn. There are three steps. Here comes step one. Step one: ask your grown-up to pick one thing in the room that makes a sound. A spoon on a cup, paper, or clapping hands. Do not look! Keep your eyes closed. Tell me when your eyes are closed and your grown-up is ready. 😊

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: This page is your Quick Reference — it holds all the important science words for Unit 3, Ourselves. Today I am your teacher, and we will learn these words so you can say them and use them. By the end, you will be able to touch a body part, name it, and say what it does. You need nothing but your own body and your voice. A grown-up can sit near you if you like. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Stand up. Touch each part and say its name out loud: head, arms, legs, hands, feet. I expect you to say all five words out loud, one for each part you touch. Then type them back to me in the order you touched them. Take your time — there's no rush.

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text:
Today we are doing our first experiment: The Mystery Sound. 🔎

You will close your eyes and use only your ears to find a sound. We do this to learn how our senses tell us about the world, even when we cannot see. By the end you will be able to say which sense helped you, and why ears are so useful. You need: your ears, a grown-up or a family member to help, and one thing that makes a sound, like a spoon and a cup. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Get ready. Sit down and ask your grown-up to hold something that makes a soft sound. They should stand somewhere in the room without telling you where. What I expect from you: tell me what sound-maker you chose. A spoon, keys, or clapping hands all work well. Tell me when you are ready!

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Welcome to Guided Practice! I am your teacher today. This page is where we practise everything about our bodies and our five senses. We practise so the words stay in your head, ready for the quiz later. By the end you will be able to name body parts, name the five senses, and say how they keep you safe. You need only two things: your own body to touch and point at, and your voice to answer me. Here is what I expect from you. Answer with the body part, and try to say it in a full sentence, like "We hear with our ears." If you do not know, say "I'm stuck" and I will give you a hint, not the answer. There are twelve questions. We will do them one at a time, slowly. Here comes question one. Which part of your body do you use to see?

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Welcome to Science Fluency! This is our quick-answer game about our bodies and our five senses. We do it so the answers come fast, without you having to stop and think hard. Like knowing your own name! There are twelve questions, in three rounds. I will ask one at a time, and wait for you. What I want from you: say your answer in your own words. Do not worry about spelling. Guessing bravely is allowed — mistakes are how we learn. Here comes question one. Which part of your body do you use to see?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Welcome! This page is called Solve Real Problems. It gives you little real-life questions about your body and your senses, and you answer them like a scientist. We do it because knowing your senses helps you stay safe and healthy every day. There are six problems. I will give you one at a time, and you tell me your answer in your own words. A good answer names the body part or the sense, and says a little bit of why. All you need is your voice and your own body to point at. Ready? Here comes question one. Name the five senses.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Welcome! Today we are doing "Explain Your Thinking."

In this activity you do not just say the answer. You say WHY. That is what real scientists do. By the end, you will be able to name a sense and explain how it helped you. You need your body, your thinking, and your voice or a pencil. There are 4 short questions. Here comes question one. You are in the kitchen. You smell smoke. Which sense warned you? I expect two things from you: name the sense, and name the body part you used. Take your time — there's no rush.

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to the Games page! Here we play short quiz games about our body and our senses. Each game has four quick questions. Playing is a fun way to help your brain remember the words we learned, like eyes, ears, nose and senses. Here is what I expect from you: read each question, think for a moment, then tell me your answer in your own words. Guessing is okay — mistakes are how we learn. Try to say WHY you chose it too, if you can. We will do four questions, one at a time. Tap the game on your screen called "Quick Match: Head", and after each one you can press your answer on the page too. Here comes question one. Which body part do we use to see? Is it eyes, ears, nose, or hands?

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Welcome! Today we are doing Science Words for Unit 3, Ourselves. Science Words are the special words we use to talk about our body. We are learning them so you can point to a body part and say its name out loud, like a real scientist. By the end you will know ten words: head, arms, legs, hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, mouth and senses. What I expect from you: stand up if you can, touch the part with your hand, say the word out loud, and then type it back to me. Short answers are perfect. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1 — three words. Head is the top part of your body, above your neck. Arms are the two long parts joined to your shoulders. Legs are the two long parts you stand and walk on. Touch your head, then your arms, then your legs. Say each word out loud. Then tell me: how many arms do you have?

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Welcome to Unit 4! I'm your teacher today. This unit is called Materials in my World. A material is what a thing is made from — like wood, metal, plastic or cloth. We are doing this so you can look at any object and say what it is made from, and say how it feels. Here is what I expect from you: pick up real things near you, use your fingers, and tell me what you notice in your own words. Short answers are perfect. You only need your hands and your eyes. If you want to touch something in the kitchen, ask your grown-up first. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look around you and pick up ONE thing that is safe to hold. A spoon, a toy, a book, a shoe — anything. Tell me what you picked. A good answer names the object, like "I picked a spoon."

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our lesson: Materials in my World. A material is what a thing is made from. Wood, metal, plastic, glass, cloth. In this lesson you will learn to name materials and say how they feel. By the end, you will be able to pick up any object and say what it is made from. You just need your eyes, your hands, and your voice. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Look around you. Pick up ONE thing that is near you. It could be a spoon, a cup, a toy, or a book. Tell me what you picked up. That is all I need for now.

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Hello! Today we are learning our Science Words for Unit 4. These are the words we use to say how a material feels. A material is what something is made from, like wood or metal or cloth. Why do we do this? Because a scientist needs good words to describe what they touch and see. By the end, you will be able to touch something at home and say exactly how it feels. You need your hands, your eyes, and things around you to touch. There are six words, so we have six little steps. For each one I will teach the word, and then it is your turn to find something and tell me. Step 1 of 6: Hard. Hard means it does not press in. It stays firm. A stone is hard. Now you try. Find one thing near you that is hard. Press it with your finger. What did you find?

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Explore the Concept in Unit 4, Materials in my World. In this activity we look at the things around us and find out what they are made from. We do this because everything you touch — your cup, your chair, your shirt — is made from a material. By the end you will be able to name a material and say how it feels. You need your two hands, your eyes, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. That is all! Here is what I expect from you: pick up real things, feel them, and tell me your answer in a few words. A good answer names the thing and its material, like "my spoon is made from metal". There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Look around you right now. Find one thing you can hold safely in your hand. Tell me what it is.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this page is Visual Models. A visual model is a picture that helps us see a science idea. On this page there are four pictures. They show us four big ideas about materials: what things are made from, how they feel, why we pick a material for a job, and how we sort things. We do this so you can look, touch, and say the science words out loud. By the end, you will be able to name a material and describe it. You will need your eyes, your hands, and a few small things from around you. I would like you to answer me in your own words each time — even one or two words is great. There are 4 steps. Here comes step 1. Look at the first picture, What Is It Made From? Now pick up one small thing near you. Tell me what it is, and what material it is made from. Wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper or cloth?

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Lovely — let's begin! 🙂

This page is called Worked Examples. A worked example is a question with the answer shown, so we can see how a good scientist thinks. We are doing this to practise two things: naming the material an object is made from, and using feeling words like hard, soft and bendy. Here is what I expect from you. I will show you one question at a time. You have a try FIRST, in your own words — even a guess is good. Then we look at the answer together. There are 8 examples, so we will go slowly. You need nothing but your thinking, and maybe your eyes to look around the room. Step 1. Here comes question one. A cooking sufuria is a big cooking pot. What material do you think it is made from?

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text:
Hello! I'm your teacher today, and this page is our Guided Practice for Unit 4, Materials in my World. 🌟

Practice means we try questions together, one at a time, so the ideas stick in your head. By the end you will be able to name what things are made from, like wood, metal, plastic or cloth, and use feeling words like hard, soft and bendy. Here is what I expect from you: answer in your own words, even if you are not sure. A guess is welcome! Mistakes are how we learn. You just need your eyes, your hands, and things around your home to touch. There are 12 little questions. We start with the easy warm-ups. Here comes question one. A cooking sufuria is made from which material?

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are learning a method. A method is the way scientists do a test, step by step. Our test is called "Which Material Is Waterproof?" Waterproof means water cannot get through it. By the end you will be able to guess first, then test, then say if your guess was right. Here is what I expect from you: try each step, use your eyes and fingers, and tell me what you see in your own words. There are 4 steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Get your things. Ask your grown-up for a small bowl of cold water. Then find three flat things: a piece of paper, a piece of plastic (like a plastic bag), and a piece of cloth. Tell me when you have all three, and say what they are. 🙂

games.label: Games
games.text:
Hello! Today we are going to play the Unit 4 games together. 🎲

These games are about materials — that means what things are made from — and about property words like hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. Each game gives you four quick questions. We play them so those words stick in your head, and so you can look at any object and say how it feels. Here is what I expect from you: read each question, pick your answer yourself, and tell me WHY you picked it. Even one small reason is great. You will need your eyes on the screen, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are 4 steps. Let's start with something small. Step 1: Look at your Games page and pick any one game to start. Tell me the name of the game you chose.

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Quick Reference page. This page holds our six science words for Unit 4: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff. These are describing words for materials — they tell us how a thing feels. By the end you will be able to touch something and say the right science word for it. What I expect from you: use your hands, and answer in your own words. Even one or two words is fine. You will need your fingers and things near you, like a pillow, a cup or a spoon. You can ask your grown-up to help you find them. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step one: hard and soft. Hard means it does not press in. Soft means it presses in easily. Find one hard thing and one soft thing near you. Press each one with your finger. Then tell me: what did you find? 😊

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are doing the experiment called Which Material Is Waterproof? Here is what it is. We will drop a little water on different materials and watch what happens. Waterproof means water cannot get through. We do this because it helps us choose the right material for a job — like why a raincoat is plastic and not cloth. By the end, you will be able to say which material keeps water out, and why. What I expect from you: guess first, look carefully, and tell me what you SEE. There is no wrong guess in science — a guess is called a prediction. You will need a grown-up to help with the water. You also need a piece of paper, a piece of cloth, and a plastic bag. There are four steps. Here is step one. Go and collect your three pieces: paper, cloth, and plastic. Lay them side by side on a plate or a tray. Then tell me you have them ready.

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Welcome to Solve Real Problems! On this page you use what you know about materials to answer real-life questions, like why a raincoat is made from plastic. We do this because scientists do not just name things — they explain WHY. By the end, you will be able to say what an object is made from and why that material is the right one for the job. You just need your thinking brain and your words. There are 6 problems, and we will do one at a time. Here comes question one. It is raining hard outside. Why is a raincoat made from plastic and not from cloth? I am hoping for two little parts in your answer: what plastic does with the water, and what cloth does with the water. Take your time — there's no rush.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explain Your Thinking."

In this activity you do not just say an answer — you say WHY. Thinking out loud like this is what real scientists do. By the end, you will be able to explain why a material is right for its job, using our words: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy, stiff. You just need your voice, and maybe a pencil to write your answer on the page. There are 4 questions. We will do one at a time. Here comes question one. Why are windows made from glass and not from wood? I am looking for two things from you: what glass can do, and why that helps. So try to say a sentence like "Glass is ... so we can ...". Take your time — there's no rush.

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! I am your teacher for this activity. This page is called Science Fluency. It is a quick-answer game about materials — the stuff things are made from. We do it so the science words come to you fast, without stopping to think hard. Here is what I expect from you: answer in a short sentence, and say the material or the feeling word, like metal, wood, hard or soft. Guessing is allowed! Mistakes are how we learn. There are 4 questions in Round 1. I will give you one at a time. Here comes question one. A cooking sufuria — a cooking pot — is made from which material?

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for our Science lesson. This lesson is called Pushes and Pulls. We will learn two big science words, push and pull, and see how they make things move, stop and turn. By the end, you will be able to look at any thing at home and say "that is a push" or "that is a pull". What you need: a bit of clear floor space, a ball or a toy car, and your own two hands. That's all! What I expect from you: try each little action with your body, then tell me what you noticed. Short answers are perfect. There are five steps. Here comes step one. Stand up in a clear space. Walk slowly, then walk fast. Then jump up high. Now tell me: when you jumped, what did your feet do to the floor? 🦶

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Welcome to our Science Words lesson! On this page we learn the special science words for Unit 5, Pushes and Pulls. We do this because when you know the words, you can explain how things move — like a real scientist. By the end, you will know what push, pull and force mean, and you will use them in your own sentences. You need your voice, and a pencil if you like writing. There are three steps. Here comes step 1. Our first word is push. A push means you move a thing away from you. Here is my example: I push the door and it goes away from me. Now you try. Tell me one thing YOU push. Say it in a full sentence, like "I push the..."

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text:
Welcome to Unit 5, Pushes and Pulls! 🎉

This page is our unit map. It shows what we will learn together, and today I will walk you through it. We are doing this because everything that moves — a door, a ball, a swing — moves because something pushed it or pulled it. By the end you will know the words push, pull and force, and you will be able to spot them all around your home. What you need: a clear space to stand, and one small toy or a ball. A pencil is handy too. What I expect from you: try each little action with your body, then tell me what you noticed in your own words. Short answers are perfect. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Stand up in a clear space. Walk slowly, then walk fast. Then jump up once. When you have done it, tell me: when you jumped, what did your feet do to the floor?

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today we are scientists exploring pushes and pulls. This activity is called Soft Push, Hard Push. You will push a ball or a toy two ways and watch what happens. We do this so you can see with your own eyes how a big push and a small push are different. Here is what I expect from you: guess first, then look carefully, then tell me what you saw. Guessing first is called a prediction, and real scientists do it too! You need one thing that rolls, like a ball or a toy car, and a clear floor. There are 4 steps. Step 1: Make your prediction. Tell me this — if I push a ball softly, and then push it hard, which push will make it go further? Take your time — there's no rush.

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are working with the Visual Models on your screen. These models are little pictures of the big ideas in Unit 5: push and pull. We will bring each picture to life with your own body and your own toys. By the end you will be able to say push or pull for the things you move every day. You need a clear space to stand, a small ball or toy car, and your voice. There are 5 steps, one for each model. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1. Stand up in your space. Move your body in four ways: walk, jump, turn around, and swing your arms. What I expect from you: do all four, then tell me one thing you noticed about your jump. Ready? Go!

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and this is our "Learn the Method" activity for Pushes and Pulls. A method is just a way of working, like a little recipe. We are learning the method for Fast and Slow, Roll and Slide. By the end, you will be able to say the idea in your own words, find it in your own home, and explain it like a scientist. You need your voice, and a small ball or a toy, and maybe a shoe. A grown-up can help you. There are 3 steps. Here comes step one. Step one: say the idea in your own words. The idea is this. A big push makes a thing go fast. A small push makes it go slow. I want you to tell it back to me in YOUR words, not mine — even one short sentence is perfect. Take your time — there's no rush.

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text:
Today we are doing Worked Examples. That means we look at a science question, and I show you how a good answer sounds. Then you get to try some yourself. We are doing this so you can say push and pull the right way, like a real scientist. A push moves a thing away from you. A pull brings a thing towards you. All you need is your voice and your hands. There are 8 examples, and we will do one at a time. Here comes example one. Watch how I think:

"You open a door by moving it away from you. Is that a push or a pull?"

I ask myself: which way did the door go? It went away from me. Away means push. So my answer is: it is a push, because a push moves something away from you. Now you try one. Push your hand out in front of you, then pull it back to your chest. Tell me: which one moved away from you?

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Guided Practice. In Guided Practice you answer questions about pushes and pulls. A push moves a thing away from you. A pull brings a thing close to you. Both are called a force. Why do we do it? Because saying the answers out loud helps the words stick in your head. What I expect from you: try each question first, even if you are not sure. Say your answer in a few words, and if you can, tell me why. Wrong answers are fine — mistakes are how we learn. There are twelve questions. We will do one at a time, and I will help you after each one. Here comes question one. You open a door by moving it away from you. Is that a push or a pull?

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for the Quick Reference page. This page is our word box for Unit 5. It holds the science words and the big ideas about pushes and pulls, all in one place. We use it so the words stay in your head, not just on the screen. By the end, you will be able to say each word and show me what it means with your own body. You need your hands, your voice, and a little space to move. There are four steps. Here comes step one! Step one: the two biggest words are push and pull. Push means you move a thing away from you. Pull means you bring a thing toward you. Now show me. Push your hands away from your body and say "push". Then bring your hands back to you and say "pull". Tell me when you have done it, and tell me which one moved AWAY from you.

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text: Today we are doing an experiment called Soft Push, Hard Push. An experiment is when we try something out to find an answer, like a real scientist. We are doing it to learn one big idea: how hard you push changes how fast a thing moves. By the end, you will be able to say why a big push and a small push are different. You need one ball or one toy car, and a clear space on the floor. If you need help finding one, ask your grown-up. There are 5 steps. Here is step one. Step 1: Put your ball or toy car on the floor in front of you. Now make a prediction. A prediction is what you THINK will happen before you try. Tell me this: if you push it softly, will it go fast or slow? Say your prediction out loud, then type it to me. 😊

games.label: Games
games.text:
Welcome to your Games page! These games are for practising Unit 5 — pushes and pulls. Each game gives you four quick questions, and you choose the right answer. We play them so the words push, pull and force become easy and fast in your head. Here is what I expect from you: read each question, think for a moment, then tell me your answer and say why you picked it. You just need your eyes, your brain, and your finger to tap on the screen. 😊

Let's start with the first game, called Quick Match: Push. It has four rounds. Here comes round one. Opening a door by pulling it is a... pull, push, lift, or drop? Tell me your answer, then tap it on your screen.

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Science Fluency. Science Fluency is quick practice. I say a question, you answer fast, using the words you learned in Unit 5: push, pull and force. It helps the words become easy, so you never have to stop and think hard. There are 12 short questions, in three rounds. Here is what I expect from you: answer in your own words, even just one or two words is fine, and try to say WHY. If you get stuck, say "hint" and I will help you. Take your time — there's no rush. You need nothing but your voice and your brain. Ready? Here comes question one. You open a door by moving it away from you. Is that a push or a pull?

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text:
Welcome to Solve Real Problems! 🌟

In this activity, we take what we learned about pushes and pulls and use it in real life — at home, at the market, outside in nature. We do this because science is not only in books. It is in your door, your ball, your toy box. By the end, you will be able to look at something moving and say what force made it move, stop or turn. You need your thinking brain, and a pencil if you want to write. There are 6 problems. I will give you one at a time. Here comes question one. At home: is opening a drawer a push or a pull? I expect one word from you — push or pull — and then tell me WHY. Take your time.

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Hello! Today I am your teacher for Explain Your Thinking. 🙂

In this activity you say your science ideas out loud, in your own words. We do it because a real scientist can explain WHY something happens, not just say the answer. By the end you will be able to talk about pushes and pulls like a scientist. You need your voice, and a pencil if you like to write. You can use our science words: push, pull, force. There are 4 questions. I will give you one at a time. A good answer says what happens AND why. Here comes question one. A ball is rolling across the floor. What could you do to make it stop?

lesson.label: The Lesson
lesson.text: Hello! Today our lesson is all about sounds. We will learn how sounds are made, how we hear them with our ears, and how to keep our ears safe. By the end, you will be able to say why things make sound, and sort sounds into loud and quiet. You will need your ears, your hands, and a grown-up nearby if you want help. I expect you to try each little activity for real, then tell me what you noticed. There are five steps. Here comes step one! Sit very still. Close your eyes and listen for one whole minute. Count the sounds on your fingers. Then tell me: how many sounds did you hear, and what were they?

words.label: Science Words
words.text: Welcome to our Science Words activity! On this page we learn the special words scientists use for sounds. We learn them so you can say WHY things make noise, not just that they do. By the end, you will know three big sound words and be able to use them in your own sentences. You need your ears, your voice, and your hand. That's all! We have 3 steps, one word each. Here comes step one. Our first word is SOUND. Sound is what we hear when something shakes the air. Now you try. Put your fingers gently on the front of your throat and hum a long "mmmmm". Then tell me: can you make a sound come out?

overview.label: Unit Overview
overview.text: Hello! Today we start Unit 6, called Sounds. This page shows what our whole unit is about: how sounds are made, how we hear them, and how some sounds are loud and some are quiet. We do this so you can notice sounds like a real scientist. By the end of this little tour, you will be able to say what makes a sound and which body part hears it. All you need is your ears, your hands, and a quiet moment. There are 3 short steps. Here comes step one. Sit very still. Close your eyes and listen for a slow count of ten. Then tell me two sounds you heard. A good answer names two different sounds, like "a bird" and "a fan". Take your time — there's no rush.

explore.label: Explore the Concept
explore.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for "Explore the Concept" in our unit about Sounds. In this activity we find out what sound is, and how our ears hear it. We do it with our own hands and our own ears, not just by reading. By the end you will be able to say what makes a sound, and tell loud sounds from quiet ones. You need three things: your ears, your hands, and a grown-up nearby if you want help. There are 5 small steps. I will give you one step, then wait for you. Step 1: Listening. Sit very still. Close your eyes. Listen for one whole minute. What I expect from you: come back and tell me at least two different sounds you heard. Even tiny ones count! Take your time — there's no rush. 🙂

visuals.label: Visual Models
visuals.text: Hello! Today we are on the Visual Models page. These are five little picture-ideas about sound, one for each big idea in our unit. We do this so the science sticks in your head as a picture, not just words. By the end, you will be able to say what makes a sound, and how it gets to your ear. You need your ears, your hands, and a grown-up nearby if you want one. That's all! There are five steps. Here comes step one. Step one: Sounds All Around Us. Sit very still. Close your eyes. Listen for one whole minute. I expect you to come back and tell me two or three sounds you heard. Take your time — there's no rush. 👂

method.label: Learn the Method
method.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on Learn the Method. This activity teaches you how a scientist works. First you guess what will happen, then you look and listen very carefully, then you check if your guess was right. We will use one little tool: a rubber band. By the end you will be able to say what makes a sound. There are 4 small steps. Take your time — there's no rush. Step 1: Find one rubber band. Ask your grown-up to help you find one. Hold it and stretch it a little between two fingers. Tell me when you have it in your hands. 🙂

examples.label: Worked Examples
examples.text: Hello! Today we are doing Worked Examples for our unit on Sounds. A worked example is a question with the answer shown, so we can see how a good scientist thinks. We do them so that when a question comes in your quiz, you already know the way to answer it. All you need is your voice, your ears, and your hands. Here is what I expect from you: try each one yourself first, in your own words. A short answer is fine. There are 8 examples, and I will give you one at a time. Here comes question one. Which part of your body do you use to hear?

guided.label: Guided Practice
guided.text: Welcome to Guided Practice, Unit 6: Sounds! In this activity you answer some short questions about sounds. We do it so the big ideas stick in your head: sounds come from shaking, we hear with our ears, and sounds can be loud or quiet. Here is what I expect from you: try each question in your own words first. A short answer is fine. Guessing bravely is good — mistakes are how we learn. You need just your ears, your voice, and a grown-up nearby if you want help writing. There are 12 questions. We start easy and get a bit harder. Here comes question one. Which part of your body do you use to hear?

reference.label: Quick Reference
reference.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher, and we are on the Quick Reference page. Quick Reference is like a little pocket card for Unit 6. It holds the big ideas and the science words for Sounds. We use it so the words stay in your head, not just on the screen. By the end you will be able to say the big sound rule and use three science words yourself. You need your ears, your voice, and a hand. A grown-up can sit with you if you like. There are 4 steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: Put two fingers gently on the front of your throat. Now hum a long "mmmmm". I expect you to tell me what you can feel under your fingers. Even one word is fine.

activities.label: Experiments
activities.text: Welcome to our experiment today! We are going to do The Shaky Rubber Band. In this experiment you will find out how a sound is made. We do it because scientists learn by trying things and watching closely. By the end, you will be able to say what makes a sound with your own eyes as proof. You need one rubber band, and a grown-up nearby to help you. There are 4 steps, and I will give you one at a time. Step 1: Before we touch anything, make a prediction. A prediction is what you THINK will happen. So tell me: if you pull a rubber band and let it go, do you think you will see it move? And do you think you will hear anything? Take your time — there's no rush.

games.label: Games
games.text: Welcome to the Games page! This is our practice playground for Unit 6, Sounds. A game here gives you four quick questions about sound. You tap the answer you think is right, and the game tells you straight away. We play these because saying an idea quickly, again and again, is how it sticks in your head. By the end you will be able to answer sound questions fast, without stopping to think hard. What I expect from you: read each question all the way to the end, pick your best answer, and if you get one wrong, tell me and we will look at it together. Guessing is fine — trying is what matters. Mistakes are how we learn. There are four steps. Here comes step one. Step 1: On your screen, find the first game. It is called Quick Match: Sound. Tap it to open it, and tell me when it starts. 🎵

problems.label: Solve Real Problems
problems.text: Welcome to Solve Real Problems! On this page you use what you know about sounds to answer real-life questions — about home, school, and outside. We do this because a scientist does not just remember words. A scientist uses them to explain the world. By the end you will be able to say why things make sound, and how to keep your ears safe. You need your thinking brain, your ears, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are 6 questions, and we will do one at a time. What I expect from you: try an answer in your own words, even if it is short. Use our science words when you can: sound, vibration, ear, loud, quiet. Here comes question one. A drum only makes a sound when you hit it. Why?

fluency.label: Science Fluency
fluency.text: Hello! Today I am your teacher for Science Fluency in Unit 6, Sounds. Science Fluency means quick practice questions about sound. We do it so the big ideas — vibration, loud and quiet, and our ears — become fast and easy in your head. By the end you will be able to answer sound questions without stopping to think hard. You need only your ears, your voice, and maybe a grown-up nearby. There are 12 questions, in 3 rounds of 4. I will give you one at a time, you tell me your answer, and I will tell you how you did. Here comes question one. Which part of your body do you use to hear?

explain.label: Explain Your Thinking
explain.text:
Welcome to Explain Your Thinking! In this activity you do not just give an answer — you say WHY. Scientists always explain their thinking, and that is what we practise today. By the end, you will be able to talk about sound, vibration and your ears in your own words. You need just two things: your voice, and your hand. 🙂

There are 4 short questions. I will give you one at a time, and I will wait for your words. A good answer says what you notice AND why. One or two sentences is perfect. Here comes question one. Put your hand gently on the front of your throat. Now hum a long "mmmmm" sound. Tell me: what can you feel under your hand?
